comments: β numerical validation — Monte Carlo check of the analytical variance
formula for the octonion associator, Fano-triple case.
Setup (per docs/research/variance_of_associator.md § "Worked example:
single Fano generator"):
A(a, b, c) := ‖[a, b, c]‖²   where [a,b,c] = (a·b)·c − a·(b·c)
Unperturbed: [a,b,c] = 2·e_7, A = 4.
Perturb a_1 → 1 + δ, δ ~ N(0, σ²). The analytical first-order GUM
variance (from the β document, derivation):
Var(A) ≈ 64 σ²                                (TRUTH)
If the current compiler's stepwise scalar-product rule were applied
instead, it would give:
Var_compiler(A) ≈ 16 σ²                       (COMPILER, 4× low)
This test computes the sample variance of A over N = 100,000 Monte
Carlo samples and compares to the TRUTH formula. It does NOT test the
compiler's variance_of() — that requires the full Knowledge<f64>
chain which introduces unrelated complexities (see ζ buffer bug). The
compiler comparison is deferred to a separate test.
Pass criterion: |MC_var − 64σ²| / 64σ² < 0.05 (5% relative error).
If this passes, β's analytical formula is validated empirically. The
remaining claim — that the compiler produces 16σ² — is then a
separate reading-confirmation task.

instruction: Write a Sounio run-pass example named `epistemic_var_accumulator_slots`. Regression pin for #1535: a mutable local must carry its uncertainty across reassignment, including when it was initialised from an EXPRESSION and when the reassignment happens inside a loop. It should compile and run successfully. Expected stdout: VAR_ACCUM_OK
description: Regression pin for #1535: a mutable local must carry its uncertainty across reassignment, including when it was initialised from an EXPRESSION and when the reassignment happens inside a loop.
comments: Regression pin for #1535: a mutable local must carry its uncertainty across
reassignment, including when it was initialised from an EXPRESSION and when the
reassignment happens inside a loop.
Two defects sat here, and the second hid behind the first:
1. Assignment REBOUND the local's variance/sens to the RHS's fresh vregs
instead of copying into fixed slots. A rebind is a compile-time map update
and a loop body's IR is emitted once, so every iteration recomputed from
the pre-loop uncertainty and only one iteration's contribution survived.
2. The fix for (1) allocated those slots BEFORE the branches that bind a
declaration's variance from its RHS, so those branches overwrote them.
Only a literal-initialised local escaped, because a literal leaves those
branches nothing to bind.
Truth values below are first-order GUM propagation, computed independently
rather than read off either engine. var(cl) = 1.24^2 = 1.5376.
TEST 1 deliberately uses NO loop. The defect never needed one — a loop only
turned a wrong answer into a catastrophic one. Four loop-based repros failed to
separate the two causes; three straight-line assignments did it immediately.
If this pin ever regresses, TEST 1 is the one that localises it.

description: Copilot review (PR #2516) finding #1 on the second review round: fo_name_hash/fo_name_hash2 (self-hosted/ir/lower.sio) used to cap their rolling hash at the first 64 bytes of the name, even though `Name.buf` is
comments: Copilot review (PR #2516) finding #1 on the second review round:
fo_name_hash/fo_name_hash2 (self-hosted/ir/lower.sio) used to cap their
rolling hash at the first 64 bytes of the name, even though `Name.buf` is
`[i8; 384]` and the parser accepts identifiers that long. Two function
names sharing a 64-byte-plus common prefix but differing only AFTER byte
64 therefore hashed identically in BOTH LOWER_FN_TUPLE_ARR_HASH and
LOWER_FN_TUPLE_ARR_HASH2, so `lower_fn_tuple_f64_array_mask` could return
one function's array-slot mask for a DIFFERENT function sharing that
truncated prefix -- exactly the bits-as-i64 (or, here, the mirror-image
bits-as-f64) corruption this whole side table exists to prevent, just
reached via a long-name collision instead of a short-name one.
The two names below share a 64-byte prefix and differ only in their last
two characters ("aa" vs "bb"). `..aa` returns a tuple of two f64 arrays
(mask = 3, both slots arrays). `..bb` returns a tuple whose slot 0 is a
plain [i64; 2] array and whose slot 1 is an [f64; 2] array (mask = 2, only
slot 1 an array). If the hash were still truncated at 64 bytes, both names
would collide in the table and `..bb`'s lookup could pick up `..aa`'s
mask (3) instead of its own (2), wrongly marking `..bb`'s INTEGER slot 0
as an f64 array too -- so reading its plain i64 elements would misread
the raw bits as f64 (the mirror image of the original kinetics bug, same
root cause: a stale/wrong mask from an unrelated function).

A tuple-returning function that CALLS another tuple-returning function used to destroy its caller's aggregate-return pointer. The x86 SRET prologue is `push rbp; mov rbp,rsp; push r12; sub rsp,frame`, so. It should compile and run successfully. Expected stdout: TUPLE_SRET_R12_OK
description: A tuple-returning function that CALLS another tuple-returning function used to destroy its caller's aggregate-return pointer. The x86 SRET prologue is `push rbp; mov rbp,rsp; push r12; sub rsp,frame`, so
comments: A tuple-returning function that CALLS another tuple-returning function used to
destroy its caller's aggregate-return pointer.
The x86 SRET prologue is `push rbp; mov rbp,rsp; push r12; sub rsp,frame`, so
the saved r12 lives at rbp-0x08 -- which was also slot 1, where the incoming
SRET pointer was stored. `pop r12` then restored that pointer instead of the
caller's r12, and the caller wrote its result through a pointer into the
callee's dead frame. The next call reused those bytes, so every binding read
the LAST call's values.
Confirmed under gdb: r12 intact at the callee's entry, holding the callee's
own SRET at its `ret`. Fixed by reserving slot 1 for the pushed r12.
Two bindings minimum: with one, a stale pointer still reads its own values.
